topics.title: Network basics
topics.note: Week 1 covers why networks matter and the vocabulary for describing them: nodes, edges, directed and weighted links, bipartite networks, adjacency matrices and edge lists.

topics.title: Degree distributions and power laws
topics.note: Weeks 1 and 2 cover how node degrees are spread out in real networks: hubs, heavy tails, log-log plots and CCDFs, and how to test whether a tail really follows a power law.

topics.title: Network visualization
topics.note: How to draw a network so it shows structure: force-directed layouts, alternatives to the hairball, landmark network pictures, and the tools students use to make their own.

topics.title: Random graphs
topics.note: Week 2 asks why we model networks at all, then builds the Erdős–Rényi random graph as the baseline: its Poisson degree distribution, the phase transition at average degree 1, and the giant component that follows.

topics.title: Small worlds and clustering
topics.note: Why any two people sit a few handshakes apart, how Milgram first measured it, how the clustering coefficient counts triangles, and how the Watts–Strogatz model gets short paths and high clustering at once.

topics.title: Preferential attachment and scale-free networks
topics.note: Week 2 covers how growth plus preferential attachment produces hubs and power-law degree distributions, why that rich-get-richer mechanism shows up far beyond networks, and the open argument over how many real networks are actually scale-free.

topics.title: Null models and the friendship paradox
topics.note: Week 2 uses degree-preserving shuffles and the configuration model to test whether a network's structure beats chance, and explains why your friends have more friends than you.

topics.title: Paths and centrality
topics.note: Week 3 covers how to find shortest paths with breadth-first search, measure distances, and rank nodes by degree, closeness and betweenness to spot brokers and bridges.

topics.title: Eigenvector centrality and PageRank
topics.note: Week 3 asks who has important friends: eigenvector centrality and PageRank score a node by the scores of the nodes pointing at it, which equals where a random surfer spends its time, and Google built its search ranking on that idea.

topics.title: Homophily, assortativity and cliques
topics.note: Week 3 asks who connects to whom: degree and attribute assortativity, homophily, how mild preferences produce segregation (Schelling), echo chambers in online networks, and cliques as the densest groups.

topics.title: Communities and modularity
topics.note: Week 4 covers how to find groups of densely linked nodes: edge betweenness and Girvan–Newman, modularity, the Louvain and Leiden algorithms, overlapping communities (k-clique and link communities), and test cases such as Zachary's karate club.

topics.title: Weak ties, weights and backbones
topics.note: Week 4 adds weights to links: why weak ties bridge groups (Granovetter), how tie strength shows up in phone and online data, and how to pull a significant backbone out of a dense weighted network.

topics.title: Text as data: tokens, Zipf and bag of words
topics.note: Week 5 turns text into numbers: splitting it into tokens, counting words and n-grams, fitting Zipf's and Heaps' laws, building the document-term matrix, and seeing what counting misses.

topics.title: TF-IDF, cosine similarity and search
topics.note: Weeks 5 and 6 turn documents into weighted word vectors with TF-IDF, compare them with cosine similarity, and use the same ideas to see how search engines rank results.

topics.title: Comparing groups and topic models
topics.note: Week 6 asks which words set one group of documents apart from another (Scattertext, log-odds with a prior, distinctive words) and what themes a corpus holds (LDA, NMF, pyLDAvis).

topics.title: Distributional semantics and word embeddings
topics.note: Week 6 treats words as known by the company they keep: count word-context co-occurrences, reweight them with PMI and PPMI, then learn dense vectors (word2vec, GloVe) whose geometry supports analogies and also carries social bias.

topics.title: Sentiment, transformers and contextual embeddings
